content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission for unit B1.2-M07. In this lesson, you will explore how professional speakers and writers connect their thoughts smoothly using advanced linkers of purpose and cause. You will read a text about a community project and see how precision in grammar makes communication clear and effective.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Using in order to and so that for purpose, and because of and due to for causes.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Vocabulary related to planning, problem solving, and formal communication.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific grammatical linkers to understand cause and effect relationships in a text.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea and specific details of a formal reading passage about community projects.
Recognize the difference between purpose connectors like in order to and so that.
Distinguish between cause connectors followed by noun phrases and clauses.

contextWarmup.prompt: When a team needs to explain why they cancelled an outdoor event, which phrase sounds most natural in a formal announcement?
options: Due to bad weather conditions, the event was postponed.
Because of we had bad weather, the event was postponed.
In order to bad weather, the event was postponed.
contextWarmup.explanation: Due to is followed by a noun phrase, which is correct for formal announcements. Option B is grammatically incorrect because because of needs a noun phrase, not a full subject and verb clause. Option C mixes purpose with cause incorrectly.

rules: IN ORDER TO + verb (infinitive): Used to express purpose with a formal structure. Example: 'She studies every night in order to pass the exam.'
SO THAT + subject + modal verb (can/could/will/would): Used to express purpose with a full clause. Example: 'He speaks slowly so that everyone can understand him.'
BECAUSE OF / DUE TO + noun phrase: Used to express cause before a noun phrase. Example: 'The flight was cancelled due to bad weather.'
BECAUSE + subject + verb (clause): Used to express cause before a full sentence clause. Example: 'They arrived late because the traffic was heavy.'

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often put a full clause right after because of or due to, which is grammatically incorrect.
commonTrap.wrong: We delayed the meeting due to it was raining.
commonTrap.correct: We delayed the meeting because it was raining, or due to the rain.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Linking Ideas with Precision

content.summary: Master formal connectors of purpose and cause to write clear, cohesive paragraphs and express complex ideas effectively.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Purpose with In Order To
blueprintItems.formula: Main Clause + in order to + Base Verb (Infinitive)
blueprintItems.example: She saved money in order to buy a new laptop.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Expressing Purpose with So That
blueprintItems.formula: Main Clause + so that + Subject + Modal (can/could/will/would) + Base Verb
blueprintItems.example: He practiced every day so that he could win the competition.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Explaining Cause with Because Of & Due To
blueprintItems.formula: Main Clause + because of / due to + Noun Phrase
blueprintItems.example: The match was postponed due to heavy rain.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always follow 'in order to' with an infinitive verb without 'to' after the preposition.
mechanicsRules.badExample: They woke up early in order caught the train.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: They woke up early in order to catch the train.
mechanicsRules.why: The phrase 'in order to' requires the base form of the verb immediately after.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'so that' when the second clause introduces a new subject followed by a modal verb.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I turned on the lamp so that see the book better.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I turned on the lamp so that I could see the book better.
mechanicsRules.why: 'So that' needs a subject and a modal verb to explain the goal clearly.

mechanicsRules.rule: Follow 'because of' and 'due to' with a noun phrase, not a full subject-verb clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She missed the bus because of she overslept.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She missed the bus because she overslept, or she missed the bus because of her late sleeping habit.
mechanicsRules.why: 'Because' introduces a clause with a subject and verb, while 'because of' requires a noun phrase.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with a logical cause using 'because of':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The sports match was postponed _______
practicumQuestions.hint: Add a noun phrase indicating bad weather or an unexpected event.
targetAnswers: The sports match was postponed because of the heavy rain.
The sports match was postponed because of bad weather.
The sports match was postponed because of strong winds.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Because of' functions as a prepositional phrase, so it must be followed by a noun phrase like 'bad weather'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct connector ('because of' or 'due to'):
practicumQuestions.promptText: Her success in the project was _______ her careful planning and hard work.
practicumQuestions.hint: Both connectors work before noun phrases, but choose the most natural fit for attributing success.
targetAnswers: due to
because of
practicumQuestions.explanation: Both 'due to' and 'because of' are grammatically correct before the noun phrase 'her careful planning and hard work'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'so that':
practicumQuestions.promptText: They left early to avoid missing the beginning of the concert.
practicumQuestions.hint: Introduce a subject and the modal verb 'would' or 'could' after 'so that'.
targetAnswers: They left early so that they would not miss the beginning of the concert.
They left early so that they could avoid missing the beginning of the concert.
They left early so that they wouldn't miss the beginning of the concert.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'So that' is followed by a clause containing a subject ('they') and a modal verb ('would' or 'could').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Find and fix the error in the sentence below:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She joined the club because of she wanted to meet new friends.
practicumQuestions.hint: Look at what follows 'because of'. Is it a noun phrase or a full clause?
targetAnswers: She joined the club because she wanted to meet new friends.
She joined the club because of her desire to meet new friends.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Because of' cannot be followed by a subject-verb clause ('she wanted'). Use 'because' for clauses or change it to a noun phrase.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the ideas into one sentence using 'in order to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Mark wore a heavy coat. He wanted to protect himself from the freezing wind.
practicumQuestions.hint: Connect the action to the purpose using 'in order to'.
targetAnswers: Mark wore a heavy coat in order to protect himself from the freezing wind.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Since Mark is the subject of both actions, 'in order to protect' smoothly joins the purpose to the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence explaining why someone studies English, using 'in order to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Write a sentence starting with: 'Many students study English...'
practicumQuestions.hint: Complete the sentence with an infinitive purpose clause.
targetAnswers: Many students study English in order to find better job opportunities.
Many students study English in order to travel around the world.
Many students study English in order to communicate with international friends.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A well-formed sentence uses 'in order to' followed by a base verb phrase explaining the purpose of studying English.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Linking Ideas with Precision

content.summary: Mastering spoken connectors such as in order to, so that, because of, and due to requires clear articulation and correct sentence stress. When speaking at a B1 level, you must link words naturally to maintain a smooth rhythm and ensure your listener understands your exact reasons and purposes.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pausing slightly before clauses of cause and purpose. Keep grammatical connectors like 'to' and 'that' unstressed and weak, while placing primary stress on nouns, verbs, and adjectives.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress on Key Content
pillars.target: Emphasize nouns and verbs while weakening functional linkers
pillars.explanation: In sentences using 'because of' or 'due to', stress the noun phrase that follows rather than the preposition itself.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.target: Link consonant endings to vowel beginnings
pillars.explanation: When saying 'due to unforeseen circumstances', link the final sound of 'due' smoothly into 'to' without a hard glottal stop.

pillars.name: Intonation in Complex Sentences
pillars.target: Use rising intonation in introductory clauses and falling intonation at the final period
pillars.explanation: If you start a sentence with 'Because of budget constraints', use a slight rise in your voice before delivering the main clause with a falling tone.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the stress shifts slightly from the second syllable in precision to the second syllable in precise, keeping the vowel clear.
Adding suffixes changes the main stress to the penultimate syllable in implementation.
Both words maintain primary stress on the second syllable.
The stress moves to the fourth syllable when forming the noun accommodation.

writing.explanation: 'Due to' must be followed by a noun phrase ('a signal failure') instead of a full subject-verb clause.

because of
